slides.narration: Welcome to Book III, Chapter 8: Organizing Unique and Keyed Data. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. In algorithms, beauty is not enough. Every procedure needs a specification, a correctness argument, a cost model, and a witness that lets us inspect behavior.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 8, treat 8.1.1 Maintaining Unique Values as an algorithmic claim. Constructing a standard ordered set from one, two, two, and four leaves the unique keys one, two, and four under ordinary integer ordering. This is useful when the application cares about presence rather than arrival multiplicity. For custom keys, comparator equivalence means neither key orders before the other, which need not be identical to an unrelated operator==. The comparison relation must remain consistent while keys are stored. Mutating a key in place so that its ordering position becomes wrong would violate the container’s organization; use the supported erase/reinsert or node-handling mechanisms when changing keys. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 8, treat 8.2.1 Associating Keys with Values as an algorithmic claim. The word-count loop uses ++counts[word] intentionally: a missing key is inserted with an initialized integer count, then incremented. Here insertion during lookup is the desired counting operation, not an accidental side effect. A read-only report should instead use find, contains, or at according to its error policy. Conflating those two use cases can inflate a map with keys that were only queried. The mapped count also needs a numeric bound for unbounded real input; the short fixture’s four words are safely representable. A map separates identity from associated information. A machine identifier can map to its last observed software version; an event category can map to a count. The key determines which entry is addressed, while the mapped value describes that entry. Two records with the same key require an update or conflict policy, not an accidental duplicate. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.title: 8.2.2 Comparing Ordered and Hash-Based Maps
keyPoints: An ordered map provides traversal by its comparator, which directly supports lexical reporting.
An unordered map organizes by hash/equality and offers no sorted traversal promise.
Both can represent the same mathematical mapping while presenting entries in different orders.
Compare contents by key rather than comparing incidental iteration sequences.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 8, treat 8.2.2 Comparing Ordered and Hash-Based Maps as an algorithmic claim. An ordered map provides traversal by its comparator, which directly supports lexical reporting. An unordered map organizes by hash/equality and offers no sorted traversal promise. Both can represent the same mathematical mapping while presenting entries in different orders. Compare contents by key rather than comparing incidental iteration sequences. If deterministic sorted output is required from an unordered map, materialize and sort a report or choose an ordered map. The right choice depends on lookup frequency, updates, ordering needs, memory, and key-operation costs—not solely on a headline average lookup bound. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 8, treat Evidence and interpretation as an algorithmic claim. The intersection is two and four, the union is one through four, and the left difference is one. These exact result vectors verify both content and the sorted output order produced from the chosen ordered inputs. The word read appears twice, while test and build appear once. That distinction is useful when replacing an implementation: the external contract may require only content, or it may additionally require a specific report order.
